mcqs.question: A table is perfectly fresh (updated on schedule) and has a normal row count, but a percentage column suddenly contains values over 100. Which observability pillar catches this?
options: Freshness, since the update timing is what matters most
Volume, since row count anomalies cover all data problems
Schema, since a percentage over 100 always indicates a type mismatch
Distribution, which checks whether the actual values in a column look statistically normal, independent of freshness or volume being fine
mcqs.explanation: This is exactly the case the distribution pillar exists for — freshness and volume can both look completely normal while the values themselves have gone statistically wrong, which is a distinct failure mode from timing or count. Freshness and volume are both fine in this scenario by definition, and a percentage over 100 is a value-range problem, not necessarily a type mismatch that a schema check would catch.

mcqs.question: A freshness monitor is configured with a flat threshold that doesn't account for a table only updating on business days. What's the likely consequence?
options: The monitor will correctly distinguish weekends from real staleness automatically

The monitor will either cry wolf every weekend or be set loose enough to miss real staleness during the week — getting the expected-cadence model right, including legitimate quiet periods, is the actual work
The monitor will simply stop running on weekends without any configuration change
Freshness monitors cannot be configured for tables with irregular update schedules
mcqs.explanation: A flat threshold forces a bad trade-off between two failure directions — false alarms every weekend, or a threshold loosened enough to also miss genuine staleness on a weekday — which is exactly why modeling the expected cadence correctly, including its normal quiet periods, is most of the real engineering work. The monitor doesn't automatically detect the pattern or pause itself on weekends without being told to, and irregular schedules are configurable — the difficulty is doing it correctly, not an inherent limitation.

mcqs.question: A volume anomaly monitor fires because today's row count spiked well above the baseline. What does this alert, by itself, tell you?
options: That the underlying data is definitely correct and the spike is a false positive
That the spike must be caused by a pipeline bug, since legitimate business events never cause volume spikes

Only that something changed relative to the expected baseline — it doesn't distinguish a genuine business event (a traffic surge) from a pipeline bug (a fan-out join), which still requires human investigation
That a specific join in the pipeline has started duplicating rows
mcqs.explanation: The alert signals deviation from baseline, full stop — it looks identical whether the cause is a real, benign business event or an actual bug, so distinguishing between them is exactly the follow-up work a human still has to do. It isn't proof of correctness, legitimate business events absolutely can cause real volume spikes, and the alert alone doesn't pinpoint a specific mechanism like a particular join without further investigation.

mcqs.question: A pipeline's infrastructure dashboard shows all metrics green — no errors, normal CPU and memory. What does this tell you about whether the data itself is correct?
options: It guarantees the data is correct, since infra health and data health are the same signal
It guarantees the data is stale, since healthy infra usually means the job finished too quickly

Nothing on its own — infra observability watches the systems moving data, not the content of the data itself, so a pipeline can be infra-healthy while producing stale, incomplete, or statistically wrong output
It only applies to batch pipelines, not streaming ones
mcqs.explanation: Infra metrics and data-content correctness are structurally different signals — a job can succeed by every infrastructure measure while a silent logic bug corrupts every row it writes, which is exactly the gap data observability closes. Green infra doesn't guarantee correctness or imply staleness, and the same principle applies to streaming pipelines just as much as batch ones.

mcqs.question: A recent deploy introduces a join condition that duplicates every row with more than one match. Why does this not show up as an error in any infrastructure log?
options: Row duplication always triggers a distinct, well-known infrastructure error code
The job completes successfully by every infrastructure measure because the bug is in the business logic's correctness, not in anything the infrastructure layer is designed to detect
Infrastructure monitoring specifically checks for duplicate rows as one of its core metrics
This kind of bug is impossible to introduce without also crashing the job
mcqs.explanation: Infrastructure monitoring checks whether systems behaved normally (no crash, normal resource use), which is a completely different question from whether the data's content is logically correct — a duplicating join produces more rows, not an error, so nothing at the infra layer has any reason to flag it. There's no such error code, infra monitoring doesn't inspect row-level duplication as a metric, and this exact kind of logic bug is a common, non-crashing failure mode.

mcqs.question: A distribution anomaly investigation reveals an undocumented business logic assumption that turned out to be wrong. What should happen to that finding beyond resolving the immediate incident?
options: Nothing further — once the immediate incident is resolved, the investigation is complete
The finding should feed back into the pipeline's quality checks or contract coverage, so the same failure is caught automatically next time rather than requiring another manual investigation
The monitor that caught it should be disabled, since it already did its job once
The finding should only be shared informally, since formalizing it would be redundant with the monitor that already caught it
mcqs.explanation: Closing the loop back into quality checks and contracts is what turns a one-time manual catch into a permanent, automated one — otherwise the same class of failure can recur and require the same manual investigation all over again. Treating the investigation as done, disabling the monitor, or keeping the finding informal all throw away the chance to prevent a repeat of the same problem.
